success_patterns: In all 5 trajectories the answer is the entity or headword repeated in many passage titles ([TLE]) alongside the clue's distinctive words: 'Encyclopedia Brown', 'Funny Girl', 'The Polar Express', 'Fume', and Neoprene pages glossing 'synthetic rubber'. The agents took that recurring title entity, even when no archive line gave the answer.

Fragment-style clues were resolved to the right slot type. A quoted epithet ('America's Sherlock Holmes in Sneakers') gave the person or character it describes. A 'YEAR: Starring X' fragment gave the film title only, with no year or actor. 'It can mean to A or to B' gave the single dictionary headword in base form.

Formatting followed the existing rules. 'material' gave bare 'rubber', dropping 'synthetic'. A quoted word that ends a title ('Express') gave the full title with its leading article, 'The Polar Express'. A word-sense clue gave the headword 'fume', not one of the definition words ('emit').

patch.reasoning: Every success relied on a signal the skill only partly states: the passage titles. The entity or headword that recurs across several titles together with the clue's distinctive phrase is the answer. The fragment shapes (quoted epithet, 'YEAR: Starring X', 'can mean A or B') and the quoted-title-word case are not spelled out and are worth a short bullet each. The edits are compact to avoid the dilution seen in rejected earlier steps.

edits.target: Do not choose one that fits only some.
edits.content: - Passage TITLES ([TLE]) are strong evidence. When there is no verbatim archive answer (or the snippets only repeat the clue), find the entity or headword that recurs across several titles alongside the clue's distinctive words ('Encyclopedia Brown ... America's Sherlock Holmes in sneakers' -> Encyclopedia Brown; 'Funny Girl (1968)' pages -> Funny Girl; dictionary pages titled 'fume' -> fume). Take that recurring entity rather than a word from the clue or from a one-off passage.

edits.target: and answer with the common English name (Conch).
edits.content: - Quoted epithet or tagline with no 'this' ('He's "America's Sherlock Holmes in Sneakers"') asks WHO or WHAT carries that label. Answer with the person, character or thing the passages pair with the tagline (Encyclopedia Brown). Category-style fragments of the form 'YEAR: <descriptor>' ('1968: Starring Barbra Streisand') ask for the work of that year that fits the descriptor. Give only the title (Funny Girl), not the year, the star or the studio.

edits.target: use your own knowledge of sports terms and idioms.
edits.content: - Word-sense clues ('It can mean to emit vapor or to show irritation', 'a synonym for...') describe one dictionary headword. Dictionary snippets (Dictionary.com, Merriam-Webster, Free Dictionary) list both senses under the same title word. Answer that headword in base form (infinitive without 'to': 'fume'). Never answer with a word from the definition ('emit', 'vapor') or a related noun sense unless the headword is that noun.

edits.target: The 'do not repeat clue words' rule is for a separate modifier already stated in the clue ('hasty' + pudding).
edits.content: - A word in quotation marks that ends the clue ('his book about this "Express"') is the last word of a title. Give the full title with its leading article as the passages print it ('The Polar Express'), because the bare quoted word is not a title. By contrast, 'X is a synthetic type of this material' wants only the bare material ('rubber'), with no 'synthetic'.
